sum: Investing.com -- Barclays downgraded A.P. Moller-Maersk to Underweight from Equal Weight and slashed its price target to 17,500 Danish kroner from 25,000, saying the risk-reward has turned negative as higher investment needs weigh on free cash flow.
The change is "less about near-term earnings, which remain supported, and more about medium-term risk-reward," analyst Marco Limite wrote.

Limite gave five reasons for the downgrade. First, management said at the third quarter that "there are more opportunities today to reinvest into the business than there was just a few years ago," pointing to capex above the roughly $5 billion historical average. Lease costs should also rise in 2027, with the existing fleet at about 95% utilization, and from 2028 up to 70% of vessel delivery capex is paid in the year of delivery.

Second, buybacks have moved down the capital allocation list. A larger buyback had been one of Barclays' positive catalysts, but with capex needs rising and balance sheet flexibility a priority, Limite sees a lower chance of meaningful support.

Third, 2026 tailwinds from strong demand and supply congestion could normalize in 2027, putting pressure on rates. Limite said strong Chinese exports, driven by AI, electric vehicles and green technology, could be hit by AI-related regulation and potential EU-China trade barriers.

Fourth, investor expectations already seem to reflect a solid 2027, with only a modest earnings decline. Barclays forecasts 2027 EBITDA of $12.5 billion, $1.5 billion below 2026, and sees no significant upside risk.

Fifth, the 2028 earnings trough is moving into view. Newbuild deliveries add about 10% to industry capacity in 2027, which looks manageable, but a further 17% in 2028 "will be much harder to absorb," the analyst wrote.

sum: Cosco Shipping Holdings reported an 80.73% increase in third-quarter profit attributable to shareholders to approximately $2.58 billion, as revenue growth on major international shipping routes outpaced gains in cargo volumes. Profit more than doubled from the previous quarter, the China-based company (601919.SS) said.

Operating revenue rose 29.39% from a year earlier to approximately $11.34 billion, while earnings before interest and taxes increased 69.61% to $3.47 billion. The strong performance brought profit attributable to shareholders for the first nine months of 2026 to approximately $4.59 billion, up 13.22% year on year.
The earnings surge came as geopolitical disruptions forced ships onto longer voyages, supporting container freight rates. Trans-Pacific services provided the company's biggest growth driver.
Cosco's trans-Pacific revenue increased 61.20% in the third quarter, compared with cargo-volume growth of 12.98%. On Asia-Europe services, revenue rose 25.74%, while volumes increased 14.64%.

Across its container-shipping business, Cosco transported 7.21 million twenty-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, up 4.46% from a year earlier. Revenue from the segment climbed 30.35% to approximately $10.98 billion.

The company said it adjusted capacity on U.S. Southwest and Asia-Europe routes and strengthened coordination between shipping and port operations. It also expanded services in Latin America, Africa and Southeast Asia to broaden its global network.
Operating cash inflow reached approximately $7.18 billion in the first nine months, an increase of 19.83%. Cosco's debt-to-asset ratio stood at 41.36% at the end of September.

What Investors Got Wrong Before A.P. Møller Mærsk's Rally
sum: If you had been weighing A.P. Møller - Mærsk on 6 November 2025, the headlines were full of guidance tweaks, Red Sea route changes and fresh worries about overcapacity. For A.P. Møller - Mærsk shareholders, the return over the past year was 61.9%, including dividends. If you were deciding whether to buy at that point, how would you have balanced booming e-commerce logistics plans against concerns that freight strength was built on disruptions that could fade?
The Two Stories Investors Had To Choose Between On A.P. Møller - Mærsk

The shares cost DKK12,735 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at A.P. Møller & Mærsk then was really choosing between two very different stories about how global trade and e-commerce would shape its future.

The bullish view pointed to a Fair Value of DKK14,435, a price level implied by assumptions that digital efficiency, premium end to end logistics contracts and green shipping investments would support earnings resilience even if revenue decreased by 0.8% a year and profit margins fell toward 0.2%.

The more cautious camp worked off a Fair Value of DKK11,802, based on expectations that revenue would decline 3.6% a year and that reliance on Chinese export strength, rising capital expenditure and industry overcapacity could limit Maersk to a 2.3% profit margin and a 24.7x P/E in 3 years.

Maersk’s Q3 2026 report gave the bullish story fresh support. Revenue was US$18,095m against US$14,206m a year earlier, with net income at US$2,986m versus US$1,047m. Net margin moved from 7.4% to 16.5%, which challenged the cautious view that profitability would compress quickly.

The lesson is simple. When a thesis hinges on margin pressure or resilience, watch the reported net margin first, and then test any freight rate or capacity claims against that line before debating the P/E.

Congestion Pays: Maersk's Third Guidance Upgrade and the Uncomfortable Economics of Disrupted Ports
sum: Container lines from Copenhagen to Shanghai are lifting profit forecasts on the back of slow ports, long routes and tight capacity. The same disruptions that fill their income statements are draining the margins of exporters, and the analysts who see the boom now give it an expiry date: 2027.

On Thursday morning in Copenhagen, A.P. Moller-Maersk did something it has now done three times this year. It told investors it expects to earn more than it said it would. The group now guides to underlying EBITDA of between $14.0 billion and $14.5 billion for 2026, up from a range of $10.5 billion to $12.5 billion, and to underlying EBIT of $8.0 billion to $8.5 billion, up from $4.5 billion to $6.5 billion.

The market sold the shares. By the start of European trading they were down about 11 per cent. The explanation, offered by analysts quoted by Reuters, was that the upgrade had been expected and that third quarter earnings fell short. Maersk reported EBITDA of $4.7 billion, up 75 per cent from a year earlier but below the $5.04 billion consensus compiled by LSEG.

A record raise greeted by a sharp fall is a useful puzzle to start from, because the answer to it says something important about who is currently being paid for what in global shipping. The profits are real. They come from scarcity, not growth. And the scarcity is produced, in large part, by the bottlenecks that ports, exporters and consumers are paying to endure.

Maersk's own account of the quarter is candid about the source. The company said a severe typhoon season in Asia caused substantial port congestion that absorbed a sizeable amount of vessel capacity, and that average global port waiting times peaked at 16.6 hours, the highest since January 2023. The Shanghai Containerised Freight Index rose an average of 46 per cent in the third quarter compared with the second. As this column reported in August, the sequence of typhoons that hit Chinese ports that month left backlogs that the system had barely cleared before the next storm arrived.
The financial effect was sharp. Maersk's Ocean division generated EBIT of $2.6 billion, against $567 million a year earlier. Group revenue rose 27 per cent to $18.1 billion.

sum: A.P. Moller Capital is expanding its international ports portfolio through agreements to buy Singapore-based Portek International and a majority stake in Euroports, adding exposure to container terminals and the infrastructure that moves Europe’s industrial and agricultural commodities.

The infrastructure investment manager and sister company to the Danish liner operator agreed on October 15 to acquire 100% of Portek from Japan’s Mitsui & Co. through its Emerging Markets Infrastructure Fund II. The announcement came less than three weeks after its September 28 agreement to acquire control of Euroports through a separately managed investment vehicle.
Financial terms were not disclosed. Both transactions remain subject to closing conditions and approvals.

The acquisitions extend A.P. Moller Capital’s strategy of investing in essential trade infrastructure, broadening its exposure to the terminals and logistics networks that move industrial and agricultural commodities as well as containers. Euroports strengthens its European bulk and breakbulk presence, while Portek adds a geographically dispersed terminal network across Africa, Asia and Europe.
The agreements follow A.P. Moller Capital’s investment in Spanish port and logistics operator Berge, extending a portfolio assembled through stakes in established operating companies.

Portek has interests in seven terminals across Africa, Asia and Europe, giving A.P. Moller Capital additional exposure to container, vehicle and multipurpose cargo operations. Its portfolio spans Algeria, Gabon, Indonesia, Latvia, Malta and Vietnam, alongside port engineering and maintenance services.

“Portek is a strong fit with our investment strategy and active owner philosophy,” Semih Gokmen, a partner at A.P. Moller Capital, said in the acquisition announcement. “It is an established business with a diversified portfolio of port operations serving important trade flows across three continents, supported by experienced local operating teams.”

A Warmer Cold War
sum: The attack on refrigeration was a reminder to ponder the vulnerability of equipment bought from manufacturers based in unfriendly countries.

A major cyberattack has hit supermarket fridges and freezers in a number of European countries, stirring understandable suspicions of yet another Russian “gray zone” onslaught. It follows an earlier, similar attack on some 700 French supermarkets in September in which hackers caused cooling units to heat up to over 100 degrees Fahrenheit, setting off fires and spoiling food. Damage was estimated to have run into the tens of millions of euros.

In recent years we have learnt that lengthy, efficient supply chains can be a source of vulnerability. The same is clearly true of hyper-connected businesses, not to speak of the internet of things. However annoying and costly, an attack on refrigeration units is obviously no Pearl Harbor, but it is not much of a stretch of the imagination to think that it was a dress rehearsal for something.
The attack was also another reminder to ponder the vulnerability of equipment, whether it’s buses in Norway or inverters used in solar power, bought from manufacturers based in unfriendly countries.
Here’s the Washington Post from December last year on the inverters:

More than 85 percent of the utilities surveyed confidentially by the research group Strider Technologies are using inverter devices made by companies with ties to the Chinese government and military. Many cybersecurity experts warn that the devices are vulnerable to hacking that can set off cascading outages.

Chinese officials say the warnings are unfounded. The researchers, however, found evidence that engineers in China have been studying how vulnerabilities in the U.S. grid could be exploited. While such studies are common in the industry — scientists around the globe routinely share knowledge on power grid resilience — some of the Chinese efforts unnerve U.S. officials in the context of China’s broader initiatives to infiltrate infrastructure.

items.t: Vietnam Rail Freight Tie Up Could Matter For Maersk Stock (CPSE:MAERSK B)
sum: APM Terminals, part of A.P. Møller Mærsk, has agreed to work with Vietnam’s Hateco Group on a rail freight network linking industrial parks, seaports and inland logistics hubs to support domestic and cross border cargo flows.

The project gives Maersk another test case for deeper integration between ocean, rail and inland logistics, which could matter for execution risk, asset utilization and the balance between capital spending and steady profitability in its integrated logistics model.
We will look at how A.P. Møller Mærsk's investment narrative is shaped by this Vietnam rail network push into integrated logistics.

A.P. Møller - Mærsk appeals to shareholders who buy into an integrated logistics story, where ports, vessels, rail and warehousing all link into one network. The short term focus sits on whether earnings pressure, weaker net margins at 4.1% and forecast declines can be cushioned by efficiency gains from projects like Gemini and tighter capital discipline.

The Vietnam rail freight news looks incremental rather than transformational. It adds another proof point that management is leaning into end to end logistics, but it does not obviously change the main near term swing factors. Freight rate normalization, high capex needs and industry overcapacity still look like the biggest execution and earnings risks.

The most relevant context for the Vietnam initiative is the push into integrated Logistics & Services, which already contributes DKK 15,962m of revenue alongside DKK 5,563m from Terminals. The rail build out fits that pattern. It extends reach inland and could matter for asset utilization if A.P. Møller - Mærsk can keep volumes flowing across multiple transport modes.

For catalysts, the real question is whether pieces like this rail corridor let A.P. Møller - Mærsk lean less on pure Ocean freight, where earnings are forecast to decline 31.8% a year over the next three years. If integrated offerings win stickier contracts and smooth volatility, that could partially offset risks from softer freight rates and rising digital competition.

Maersk has lost both its partners on Asia–East Coast South America in three months, and what looks like a local reshuffle is the alliance map redrawing on a trade the alliances never formally covered.

In September, Zim quit Maersk’s ASAS loop to launch the AS3/ZFS with Hapag-Lloyd; yesterday, Maersk and CMA CGM said they would end their joint ASAS2/SEAS3 service, with the last sailing leaving Shanghai on 8 December; and CMA CGM is relaunching its two remaining loops, SEAS 2 and SEAS A, a few days after that.

East Coast South America (ECSA) has always been a trade on which carriers mixed freely, whatever badge they wore on Asia–Europe. From December, I expect it to look like a scale model of the alliance world.

The clearest move is Ocean Alliance closing ranks. My read is that the revised SEAS 2 and SEAS A will carry only CMA CGM, Cosco, OOCL and Evergreen – PIL and Yang Ming, long-standing members of that ECSA consortium, are out.

PIL does not go far. I expect it to join AS3/ZFS, bringing four 14,000 teu ships from its old ES1 slot. That suits Hapag-Lloyd and Zim, which are short of tonnage to complete the rotation. It also creates a third bloc built around Hapag-Lloyd, even though its merger with Zim is stuck in regulatory review.

items.t: Hapag-Lloyd Shares Jump After Second 2026 Guidance Upgrade
sum: Hapag-Lloyd shares rose 3.6% to €136.30 on Xetra after the company announced its second upward revision to full-year 2026 earnings guidance on the evening of Sept. 28.

The carrier raised its group EBITDA forecast to a range of $3.9 billion to $4.4 billion, a substantial increase from its previous projection of $2.7 billion to $3.7 billion. It also lifted its group EBIT guidance to between $1.25 billion and $1.75 billion, up from the previous range of $100 million to $1.1 billion. Management attributed the significant improvement in Hapag-Lloyd earnings guidance to persistently strong market demand and favorable conditions in spot freight rates.

On the analyst side, Barclays acknowledged the improved outlook by raising its price target for Hapag-Lloyd shares to €105, while maintaining its Underweight rating. The target remains well below the stock’s current trading level. Separately, Hapag-Lloyd confirmed the first eastbound and westbound sailings of its SE1 service through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal under the Gemini Cooperation with Maersk — a development that signals an important step toward the normalization of routes through one of the world’s most strategically important shipping corridors.

Gujarat Pipavav: A good port with a ticking clock
sum: Summary: Gujarat Pipavav Port is profitable, nearly debt-free and pays a dividend yield above 6 per cent. It trades at 14 times earnings. The discount isn't a mystery. The port has an expiry date, and nobody knows yet what happens when the clock runs out.

At first glance, there is little to dislike about Gujarat Pipavav Port (GPPL). Profits are rising, the company has almost no debt and its dividend yield is above 6 per cent. Yet the stock trades at only about 14 times earnings.

The reason is not hard to find. GPPL does not own its port outright. It operates it under a 30-year concession that expires on September 29, 2028. Until then, the business can keep earning. What happens after that is the question hanging over the stock.

GPPL operates a port on Gujarat's Saurashtra coast, handling four main cargo types: containers, dry bulk such as fertilisers and minerals, liquid cargo such as cooking gas, and automobiles. Containers are a little over half of revenue. APM Terminals, part of the Danish shipping group AP Moller-Maersk, owns 44 per cent of GPPL and is also one of its biggest customers, at roughly 19 per cent of revenue.

The business is highly profitable. In FY26, revenue rose 17 per cent to Rs 1,158 crore and profit rose 30 per cent to Rs 515 crore. Operating margins are close to 60 per cent, return on equity (ROE) about 22 per cent, and the company holds nearly Rs 700 crore in cash while paying out most of its profit as dividends.

The weakness is growth. Revenue has grown only about 6 per cent a year over the past decade. Unlike Adani Ports or JSW Infrastructure, which can expand by adding new ports, GPPL has one port on one stretch of coast, so its growth depends on handling more cargo at Pipavav.

That is becoming harder. Container volumes fell 4 per cent in FY26 even as revenue rose, so the increase was driven more by pricing than by higher volumes. Stronger cargo flows in the first quarter of FY27, partly because of disruptions in the Middle East, may not last.

sum: Aug 20, 2026 (Bloomberg) –CK Hutchison Holdings Ltd. commenced international arbitration proceedings against Panama, seeking more than $1.5 billion in damages over the loss of its investments in two ports on the country’s strategic canal.

The move came after attempts to resolve the dispute with Panamanian authorities failed, the company said in a statement Thursday. items.t: From containers to doorsteps: Maersk’s push Into parcel logistics
sum: Maersk built its reputation moving containers across oceans. Now the maritime giant wants to deliver packages to your doorstep. To do so, it’s using data modeling, artificial intelligence and a web of carrier partners to make it happen.
Sam Coiro, head of e-commerce commercial business development at Maersk, told FreightWaves the company’s push into parcels came from a simple observation: Maersk was already doing most of the work.

“Maersk is going across the world with its containers, picking things up, sailing across the ocean, moving them into warehouses, and then literally doing the fulfillment for big, big shippers. But that’s where Maersk stopped,” Coiro said. “Maersk said, ‘Wait a minute. If we’re already bringing it 75 percent of the way, doesn’t it make sense for us to do the last piece as well?’”’

That thinking sparked a series of acquisitions. Maersk bought Visible Supply Chain Management, a large parcel reseller with e-fulfillment centers across the country. It also picked up B2C Europe, a major multi-carrier shipping platform. The goal was to close the gap between warehouse and customer.

The result is Maersk Parcel — a single platform that gives shippers one label, one invoice, one rate card and one tracking experience. Behind the scenes, Maersk blends its own assets with partner carriers to move packages coast to coast.
“You can move packages from east to west, west to east, up and down, down to up,” Coiro said.

The hard part of parcel logistics isn’t forecasting Black Friday. Black Friday is always the Friday after Thanksgiving. The real challenge is the surprise demand spike that catches operators off guard.

The notice formalized a Supreme Court ruling last month that the concessions for the Balboa and Cristobal terminals near the Panama Canal, which Panama Port Co., or PPC, a subsidiary of CK Hutchison, had held for more than two decades, were unconstitutional.
